label: Introduction
title: Introduction: What These Proofs Are Trying to Do
tagline: Five old roads to one God, walked without a map of footnotes
oneSentence: Feser presents natural theology as the attempt to demonstrate God's existence by reason alone, explains how each of his five proofs moves in two stages from an undeniable feature of the world to a cause that must have the divine attributes, and stakes the bold claim that these demonstrations succeed, so that the real debate is not between atheism and theism but among theists.
bigPicture:
The introduction is short, but it sets the terms for everything that follows. Feser tells you what kind of book this is — not a commentary on Aquinas' Five Ways, not an exegesis of any historical thinker, but a direct defense of five arguments inspired by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, and Leibniz — and what kind of arguments these are. They belong to **natural theology**: the attempt to learn, by unaided reason and apart from any revelation, that God exists, what he is like, and how he relates to the world. And they aim at **demonstration** in the strong, classical sense: conclusions that follow necessarily from premises that are certain, rather than guesses about the most probable explanation.

The introduction also gives a roadmap. Chapter 1 (the **Aristotelian proof**) argues from change to a purely actual actualizer; chapter 2 (the **Neo-Platonic proof**) from composition to an absolutely simple One; chapter 3 (the **Augustinian proof**) from universals, propositions, and possibilities to a divine intellect; chapter 4 (the **Thomistic proof**) from the distinction between essence and existence to something whose essence just is existence; and chapter 5 (the **rationalist proof**) from the principle of sufficient reason to a necessary being. Chapter 6 then works out the divine nature systematically — unity, simplicity, immutability, eternity, omnipotence, omniscience, goodness, will, love, incomprehensibility — and God's ongoing relation to the world (conservation, concurrence, miracles), while chapter 7 answers the standard objections to natural theology.

Two structural promises matter for the whole course. First, every proof has **two stages**: Stage 1 shows that something fitting a key description exists (for example, an uncaused cause of the existence of things), and Stage 2 shows that whatever fits that description must have the classic divine attributes. This is Feser's answer, built into the architecture of the book, to the familiar complaint that a “first cause” is not yet God. Second, each chapter moves from an **informal** discursive statement, to a **formal** step-by-step statement, to a long section on **objections** — so a learner should never try to evaluate a formal argument without the informal explanation of its concepts.

Finally, the introduction reveals the target of the proofs and the stakes. The God in question is the God of **classical theism**, for which **divine simplicity** is central — not a very powerful person who happens to be the greatest member of a class of beings. Read with the book's later chapters, this means the arguments concern a cause that sustains the world's existence here and now, not merely a first event in the distant past, and that they are metaphysical rather than scientific or probabilistic. Feser's closing claim is deliberately provocative: demonstrative natural theology was long the mainstream of Western thought and should be again, and once it is, the serious debate is among theists of different kinds about what, if anything, God has revealed.
objectives: Define natural theology and distinguish it from theology based on divine revelation.
Explain what Feser (and the classical tradition) mean by a demonstration, and why it is not a probabilistic or “best explanation” argument like Paley-style or Intelligent Design arguments.
Describe the two-stage structure of each proof and explain why Stage 2 is essential to the book's case.
Summarize, in one or two sentences each, the starting point and conclusion of the Aristotelian, Neo-Platonic, Augustinian, Thomistic, and rationalist proofs.
Distinguish classical theism from theistic personalism and explain why the book's arguments, if sound, support only the former.
Explain why the proofs concern a cause of the world's existence here and now rather than a first event in time, and why they are philosophical rather than scientific arguments.
State what the book does and does not claim to establish (for example, it does not settle which revealed religion, if any, is true).
Reply to the objection that no one can claim a proof of God's existence because so many people reject the alleged proofs.
Explain why each chapter moves from informal statement to formal statement to objections, and why the formal statements are not meant to stand alone.

summary.heading: Not a book about the Five Ways
summary.body:
Feser begins by heading off a natural assumption. Because he has defended Aquinas elsewhere, and because the book is called *Five Proofs*, readers might expect a treatment of Aquinas' famous Five Ways (from motion, efficient causality, contingency, degrees of perfection, and finality). It is not. There is overlap with Aquinas and with Feser's own earlier work, but the ground is different.

None of the five proofs is original to Feser — all are old. What is new is that several are arguments he has not previously defended at length, and that most of them have received little attention in contemporary philosophy. That neglect is striking, he says, because these arguments were historically prominent and are, in his judgment, the most powerful arguments for God's existence available. His diagnosis is pointed: the neglect tells us nothing about the arguments and a great deal about the state of contemporary academic philosophy, including philosophy of religion. So although the arguments are ancient, they will be unfamiliar to most readers, as will much of the defense offered for them.

summary.heading: Natural theology and the limits of the earlier approach
summary.body:
Feser defines **natural theology** as the study of what unaided human reason — reason apart from divine revelation — can know about the existence and nature of God and about God's relationship to the world. In his earlier books *The Last Superstition* and *Aquinas*, he approached these questions by expounding and defending Aquinas, whom he regards as the greatest natural theologian.

That approach had advantages but also two limitations. First, it was necessarily **exegetical**: it had to explain what Aquinas meant, or how later Thomists developed his arguments. That in turn required laying out the background principles Aquinas relied on — about change, causality, contingency, and so on — and separating the essential philosophical ideas from the dated, sometimes mistaken scientific assumptions in which Aquinas occasionally expressed them. The result, in both earlier books, was roughly seventy pages of dense general metaphysics before the reader reached God at all. Second, it confined the discussion to the arguments Aquinas himself happened to regard as most important.

summary.heading: What this book does instead
summary.body:
Feser saw a twofold need: (1) a defense of important arguments for God that Aquinas does not discuss and that recent natural theology has under-examined, and (2) a presentation of all the most important arguments that skips textual exegesis and long metaphysical preliminaries, gets straight to the heart of each argument, and introduces background principles only as they are needed.

That is what the book does. Two of the five proofs can be found in Aquinas; three are not arguments he discusses, at least not at length or in the form presented. (The roadmap shows the Aristotelian proof corresponds to his First Way and the Thomistic proof to his argument in *On Being and Essence*; Aquinas also gave some expression to the Neo-Platonic idea.) There is no exegesis of Aquinas or anyone else. The proofs are inspired by Aristotle, Plotinus, Augustine, Aquinas, and Leibniz, and Feser thinks they capture what is essential in those thinkers' reasoning — but he is not interpreting their texts or claiming they would agree with all he says. It is an *Aristotelian* proof, not Aristotle's own proof exactly; an *Augustinian* proof, not a reading of what Augustine wrote. And background metaphysics is kept to the minimum, introduced along the way as the arguments require it.

summary.heading: The shape of each proof chapter: a two-stage informal statement
summary.body:
Chapters 1–5 each defend one proof, and each follows the same pattern. It begins with an **informal statement** of the argument in **two stages**.

- **Stage 1** argues that something exists which fits a certain key description — for example, “an uncaused cause of the existence of things.”
- **Stage 2** argues that anything fitting that description must have key divine attributes, such as unity, eternity, immateriality, omnipotence, omniscience, and perfect goodness.

The presentation is “informal” in that it is discursive and unhurried rather than set out in the numbered premise-and-conclusion format favored by analytic philosophers. Feser gives two reasons: he wants readers new to philosophy to be able to enter and follow the arguments, and he needs room to digress into more general metaphysical issues so as to make clear what the proofs really claim and to forestall misunderstandings and irrelevant objections. The discussion does become technical, but it introduces technicalities as gently as possible. He hopes to reach both academic philosophers and willing laypeople: every chapter ends in the deepest part of the pool, but begins in the shallowest part he can find — which, he admits, is easier for some arguments than others.

summary.heading: Formal statement and objections
summary.body:
Next comes a **more formal statement**: the argument laid out step by step, to make its logical structure as clear as possible and to recapitulate crisply what the informal section developed slowly. Feser stresses that these formal statements are **not meant to stand alone**. A reader who skips the informal discussion may misunderstand them, because it is there that the significance of each key concept is carefully explained. What the formal statement adds is a view of how everything in the informal discussion fits together.

Each chapter then ends with a long section on **objections** that have been, or might be, raised against the argument. These sections sometimes contain the book's most technical material.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 1, the Aristotelian proof
summary.body: The Aristotelian proof starts from the fact that **real change** occurs. It analyzes change as the **actualization of potential** and argues that no potential could be actualized at all unless there exists something that actualizes without itself being actualized — a **purely actual actualizer**, or what Aristotle called the Unmoved Mover. Aristotle developed such an argument in *Physics* book 8 and *Metaphysics* book 12; Maimonides and Aquinas gave their own versions, Aquinas' First Way being one. These older writers expressed the argument using archaic science, such as the motion of heavenly spheres. But, Feser says, modern Aristotelians have shown that the argument's essential kernel does not depend on that outdated husk. Chapter 1 presents the core idea as an Aristotle, Maimonides, or Aquinas might develop it today.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 2, the Neo-Platonic proof
summary.body: The Neo-Platonic proof begins from the fact that the things we experience are **composite** — made up of parts in various ways — and argues that their ultimate cause can only be something **absolutely simple** or noncomposite, what Plotinus called **the One**. The core idea is in Plotinus' *Enneads*, and Aquinas also expressed it. Feser notes that **divine simplicity** is absolutely central to the **classical theist** conception of God, yet it is strangely neglected by contemporary writers on natural theology — theists as much as atheists. One aim of the book is to restore it to its proper place.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 3, the Augustinian proof
summary.body: The Augustinian proof argues first that **universals** (redness, humanness, triangularity), **propositions**, **possibilities**, and other **abstract objects** are in some sense real. It rejects Plato's view that they exist in a “third realm” independent of every mind and of the world of particular things. The only possible ultimate ground of such objects, it concludes, is a **divine intellect** — the mind of God. The idea has Neo-Platonic roots, was central to Augustine's understanding of God, and was defended by Leibniz. Feser claims to offer a more detailed and systematic version than he knows of anyone attempting before.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 4, the Thomistic proof
summary.body: The Thomistic proof argues that in every contingent thing we experience there is a **real distinction between essence** (what a thing is) **and existence** (that it is). It then argues that nothing with such a distinction could exist even for an instant unless caused to exist by something with no such distinction — something whose very essence *is* existence and which can therefore give existence without receiving it: an **uncaused cause of the existence of things**. Aquinas presented this argument in *On Being and Essence*, and many Thomists regard it as the paradigmatically Thomistic argument.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 5, the rationalist proof
summary.body: The rationalist proof begins by defending the **principle of sufficient reason (PSR)**: everything is intelligible, having an explanation for why it exists and has the attributes it has. It then argues that the existence of contingent things cannot be explained unless there is a **necessary being** whose existence is explained by its own nature. The argument is famously associated with Leibniz, but Feser's version departs from Leibniz in several ways and interprets the key ideas in an Aristotelian-Thomistic way. It is “rationalist” in affirming PSR and the thorough intelligibility of the world, but not in other senses: it has no commitment to innate ideas or the epistemology of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, and its reading of PSR differs from theirs.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 6, God's nature and relationship to the world
summary.body:
Chapter 6 treats more deeply and systematically the themes the proof chapters already touch on. It opens with three background principles: the **principle of proportionate causality** (whatever is in an effect must in some way pre-exist in its total cause), **agere sequitur esse** (how a thing acts follows from what it is), and the Thomist account of **analogical language** about God. Using these, it first shows that all five proofs arrive at **one and the same God**, and that there can in principle be only one God. It then derives **simplicity, immutability, immateriality, incorporeality, eternity, necessity, omnipotence, omniscience, perfect goodness, will, love,** and **incomprehensibility**.

Next it defends **divine conservation** (the world could not exist for an instant unless God were continually sustaining it) and **divine concurrence** (no creature could exercise causal power unless God were imparting that power at every moment it acts). Along the way it rules out **pantheism, panentheism, occasionalism,** and **deism**. It ends with what a **miracle** is and how God might cause one — a question crucial for whether there could be knowledge of God through special revelation, though whether any revelation has actually occurred lies beyond the book's scope.

summary.heading: Roadmap: chapter 7, objections to natural theology
summary.body: Chapter 7 addresses criticisms of natural theology in general. Many will already have been handled in earlier chapters; chapter 7 takes up some not considered earlier and treats others in more depth. Feser promises that by the end it will be clear that none of the objections succeeds — indeed, that the most common ones are, in his words, “staggeringly feeble and overrated.”

summary.heading: A confident discipline, and where the real debate lies
summary.body:
Feser acknowledges this is a confident claim, but natural theology was historically a confident discipline. From the beginnings of Western thought to the present, a long line of thinkers — Aristotelians, Neo-Platonists, Thomists and other Scholastics, early modern rationalists, and others, whether pagan, Jewish, Christian, Muslim, or purely philosophical theists — held that God's existence can be **rationally demonstrated by purely philosophical arguments**. The book aims to show they were right, and that what was long the mainstream position in Western thought should become the mainstream position again.

On this view, **the real debate is not between atheism and theism** but between theists of different kinds — Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, purely philosophical theists, and so on — and that debate begins where natural theology stops. The book does not enter that debate, let alone settle it. Feser will be satisfied if it helps return us to the point from which the deepest questions can be addressed.

summary.heading: Reading ahead: foundations the introduction presupposes
summary.body:
Several ideas the introduction takes for granted are made explicit later in the book, and they are worth grasping from the start.

- **Demonstration, not probability.** In chapter 7 Feser explains that to “demonstrate” God's existence means to show that the conclusion follows with deductive necessity from premises that are certain, their certainty established by metaphysical analysis. Such arguments are not probabilistic, and not arguments to the best explanation where some rival hypothesis might in principle be correct.
- **Not design arguments.** The proofs have nothing to do with Paley-style or Intelligent Design arguments that infer a designer from biological complexity by analogy with human artifacts. A pebble or a drop of water serves the Neo-Platonic proof as well as an eye does.
- **Here and now, not back then.** The proofs concern **hierarchical** causal series operating at every moment a thing exists, not **linear** series stretching back in time; they are compatible with a universe that had no beginning. God is the sustaining cause of the world's existence, not a first domino.
- **Philosophical, not scientific.** The starting points (change, composition, abstract objects, the essence–existence distinction, contingency) are features any possible empirical inquiry presupposes, so no scientific discovery could overturn them, and the proofs are not “god of the gaps” hypotheses.
- **Classical theism, not theistic personalism.** The God concluded to is not a being among beings or the greatest member of a genus “person,” but pure actuality, absolutely simple, subsistent existence itself. In chapter 6 Feser contrasts this with the “theistic personalism” of some contemporary philosophers, and argues that nothing in his arguments would support such a merely creaturely “god.”
